pages.description: A defensive security explainer on current MCP authorization requirements and credential hygiene.
pages.content:
# Short-Lived Credentials for MCP: What Builders Need to Know

MCP authorization for HTTP-based transports follows established OAuth security patterns. The current specification defines protected MCP servers as resource servers and MCP clients as OAuth clients acting on behalf of a resource owner. Clients discover authorization infrastructure through standardized metadata rather than hard-coding arbitrary endpoints.

## Why short-lived credentials matter

Access tokens can authorize real tool and data access, so exposure can have consequences beyond a chat response. The MCP specification recommends short-lived access tokens to reduce the impact of token leakage and requires secure token storage. Public-client flows use PKCE, and resource indicators bind authorization to the intended MCP server. All authorization endpoints use secure transport requirements.

## Defensive implementation checklist

Use the current MCP specification as the source of truth. Request the minimum scopes needed for the task, keep credentials out of source control and client-visible logs, validate the intended resource, rotate or revoke credentials when access changes, and test authorization in a low-privilege environment before production rollout. STDIO deployments use a different credential model and should not copy HTTP authorization flows blindly.
